title: Isolation Levels & Read Phenomena
summary: When transactions run concurrently, anomalies appear. Isolation levels are the knob that trades correctness for concurrency.

blocks.markdown:
**Isolation** is the 'I' in [transactions-acid](transactions-acid). It controls how much one transaction can see of another's in-progress work.

- Without isolation, concurrent transactions corrupt each other's reads.
- SQL defines four levels — a dial from 'see everything' to 'see nothing in-progress'.
- Higher isolation = fewer anomalies, but more blocking and lower throughput.
- Most databases default to **Read Committed**.

**Read phenomena** are the anomalies that happen when isolation is incomplete. SQL defines three.

- **Dirty read** — reading uncommitted data written by another transaction.
- **Non-repeatable read** — re-reading the same row and getting a different value because another transaction committed between reads.
- **Phantom read** — re-running the same query and getting extra (or fewer) rows because another transaction inserted or deleted.

Each is progressively harder to prevent.

blocks.subTitle: Dirty read
blocks.markdown:
A **dirty read** occurs when transaction T2 reads a row that T1 has modified but not yet committed.

- If T1 then rolls back, T2 acted on data that never existed.
- Example: T1 sets a balance to $0 (not yet committed); T2 reads $0 and blocks a payment — then T1 rolls back and the balance is restored.
- Prevented by any level above Read Uncommitted.

blocks.subTitle: Non-repeatable read
blocks.markdown:
A **non-repeatable read** occurs when T2 reads the same row twice and gets different values because T1 committed an update between those reads.

- The row existed both times — it just changed.
- Prevented by Repeatable Read and above.

Distinction from dirty read: the data T2 saw the first time was committed; it was the second read that differed.

blocks.subTitle: Phantom read
blocks.markdown:
A **phantom read** occurs when T2 re-runs a range query and gets different rows because T1 inserted or deleted rows matching that range and committed between the two queries.

- The original rows haven't changed — new ones appeared (or vanished).
- Example: T2 counts open orders twice; T1 inserts one between counts.
- Prevented only by Serializable (and snapshot isolation handles it differently).

blocks.subTitle: Read Uncommitted
blocks.markdown:
**Read Uncommitted** — the weakest level. A transaction can read rows that other transactions have modified but not yet committed.

- Allows: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads.
- Use case: rough aggregate estimates where approximate results are acceptable.
- Almost never used in production — any rollback corrupts reads.

blocks.subTitle: Read Committed
blocks.markdown:
**Read Committed** — a transaction only sees data that other transactions have already committed.

- Prevents: dirty reads.
- Still allows: non-repeatable reads, phantom reads.
- **Default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.**
- Implemented via short-lived read locks or MVCC snapshots that advance per statement.

blocks.subTitle: Repeatable Read
blocks.markdown:
**Repeatable Read** — every row T2 reads at the start of the transaction is locked against updates for the duration.

- Prevents: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads.
- Still allows: phantom reads (new rows can appear in range queries).
- **Default in MySQL InnoDB** (though InnoDB also blocks most phantoms via gap locks).
- Implemented via longer-held read locks or an MVCC snapshot frozen at transaction start.

blocks.subTitle: Serializable
blocks.markdown:
**Serializable** — the strongest level. Transactions execute as if they ran one at a time, even if they actually overlap.

- Prevents: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads.
- Implemented via range locks, predicate locks, or serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).
- Highest correctness, highest cost — serialization conflicts abort and retry transactions.

See [serializability-recoverability](serializability-recoverability) for the formal definition.

Which level prevents which anomaly.

| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable |
|---|---|---|
| Read Uncommitted | allowed | allowed |
| Read Committed | prevented | allowed |
| Repeatable Read | prevented | prevented |
| Serializable | prevented | prevented |

blocks.subTitle: Phantom coverage
blocks.markdown:
Phantom reads need a separate view — only the top level blocks them fully.

| Level | Phantom read |
|---|---|
| Read Uncommitted | allowed |
| Read Committed | allowed |
| Repeatable Read | allowed (per SQL spec) |
| Serializable | prevented |

**Snapshot isolation (SI)** is not a SQL standard level — it's a popular implementation used by PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, Oracle, and CockroachDB.

- Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken at its start time.
- Writes are applied to the latest version, not the snapshot.
- Prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantoms — but NOT write skew.

blocks.subTitle: Write skew
blocks.markdown:
**Write skew** — a subtle anomaly SI doesn't prevent.

- T1 and T2 both read the same set of rows and make decisions based on that snapshot.
- Each writes to a *different* row, so there's no write–write conflict.
- But their combined effect violates an invariant that neither alone would break.
- Example: two doctors each see 'one on-call' and both go off-call — now zero are on-call.
- Only **Serializable** (specifically SSI) catches this.

Isolation and concurrency pull in opposite directions.

- Higher isolation → more locking or more conflict-aborts → lower throughput.
- Read Committed hits the sweet spot for most OLTP workloads.
- Bump to Serializable only for critical financial or invariant-guarding logic.

See [concurrency-control](concurrency-control) for the locking mechanisms behind these levels.

Common misconceptions:

- **'Repeatable Read prevents phantoms.'** The SQL spec says it doesn't — MySQL InnoDB happens to block most via gap locks, but that's an implementation extra, not the guarantee.
- **'Snapshot isolation = Serializable.'** SI misses write skew; Serializable (SSI) adds anti-dependency checks.
- **'Higher isolation is always safer.'** More aborts and deadlocks can crash throughput under high concurrency — tuning matters.

blocks.subTitle: Explain the four isolation levels
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Explain the four SQL isolation levels.**

Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads — almost never used. Read Committed (the common default) blocks dirty reads only. Repeatable Read also blocks non-repeatable reads. Serializable blocks everything including phantoms and guarantees serial-equivalent execution. Each step up costs more concurrency.

blocks.subTitle: Dirty vs non-repeatable vs phantom
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a dirty read, non-repeatable read, and phantom read?**

Dirty read: you see uncommitted data. Non-repeatable read: the same row returns a different value on re-read (committed update in between). Phantom: re-running a range query returns extra/fewer rows (committed insert/delete in between). Each involves a different type of interference across concurrent transactions.

blocks.subTitle: What does Repeatable Read prevent?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What exactly does Repeatable Read prevent?**

It guarantees that if you read a row once, re-reading it returns the same value — no committed update from another transaction can change it mid-transaction. It does NOT guarantee the row set for a range query stays the same (phantoms). MySQL InnoDB closes that gap with gap locks, but that's an extra, not required by the spec.

blocks.subTitle: What is snapshot isolation?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is snapshot isolation, and how does it differ from Serializable?**

Snapshot isolation gives every transaction a frozen read view from its start time — no dirty or non-repeatable reads, and no phantoms. But it can't detect write skew, where two transactions read the same snapshot and write to different rows whose combined effect breaks an invariant. Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) adds anti-dependency tracking to catch that.
